claim: Six Selected populations were maintained for over 230 generations on a nutrient-poor larval diet.
source: We compare six replicate populations (the 'Selected' populations) evolved for over 230 generations on a very nutrient-poor larval diet, to six populations of the same origin maintained on a moderately nutrient-rich standard larval diet (the 'Control' populations).
evidence: Stated directly in the manuscript text describing the experimental design.

claim: Compared to Control populations, Selected populations evolved major changes in adult gene expression and metabolite abundance.
source: Compared to Control populations maintained on standard diet, Selected populations maintained for over 230 generations on a nutrient-poor larval diet evolved major changes in adult gene expression and metabolite abundance, in particular affecting amino acid and purine metabolism.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq and metabolomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The evolutionary regime affected adult expression of about 26% of all 8701 genes included in the analysis.
source: Based on the estimation of true nulls (Storey and Tibshirani, 2003), the evolutionary regime (i.e., Selected versus Control) affected adult expression of about 26% of all 8701 genes included in the analysis while the larval diet affected about 45%.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of RNAseq data using the method of Storey and Tibshirani, 2003.

claim: 219 genes were identified as differentially expressed between Selected and Control populations at 10% FDR.
source: Allowing for 10% false discovery rate (FDR), we identified 219 genes as differentially expressed between Selected and Control populations and 827 between flies raised on standard or poor diet (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of RNAseq data with FDR correction.

claim: The larval diet affected about 45% of all 8701 genes included in the analysis.
source: Based on the estimation of true nulls (Storey and Tibshirani, 2003), the evolutionary regime (i.e., Selected versus Control) affected adult expression of about 26% of all 8701 genes included in the analysis while the larval diet affected about 45%.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of RNAseq data using the method of Storey and Tibshirani, 2003.

claim: 827 genes were identified as differentially expressed between flies raised on standard or poor diet at 10% FDR.
source: Allowing for 10% false discovery rate (FDR), we identified 219 genes as differentially expressed between Selected and Control populations and 827 between flies raised on standard or poor diet (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of RNAseq data with FDR correction.

claim: Genes differentially expressed between Selected and Control populations are enriched in cuticle development and maturation.
source: The strongest statistical signal from Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis on genes differentially expressed between Selected and Control flies points to genes involved in cuticle development and maturation, including several structural cuticle proteins (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2, table A).
evidence: Based on GO enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Most cuticle-related genes show higher expression in Selected compared to Control populations.
source: Most of these genes are mainly expressed in epidermis (including in the tracheal system), and nearly all show higher expression in the Selected compared to Control populations.
evidence: Based on analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Genes expressed mainly in hemocytes are downregulated in Selected flies.
source: Several other enriched GO terms (phagocytosis, pigment metabolic process, iron ion homeostasis, response to fungus) include multiple genes expressed mainly in hemocytes; these genes are downregulated in Selected flies, suggesting lower abundance of hemocytes.
evidence: Based on GO enrichment analysis and gene expression patterns.

claim: Differentially expressed genes are enriched in metabolic processes including oxidation/reduction, biosynthesis of purine compounds, and amino acid catabolism.
source: The other top enriched GO terms point to metabolic processes, notably oxidation/reduction, biosynthesis of purine compounds, and amino acid catabolism (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Of 113 metabolites analyzed, 57 were differentially abundant between Selected and Control flies at 10% FDR.
source: Of the 113 metabolites, 57 were found to be differentially abundant between Selected and Control flies at 10% FDR, and also 57 differentially abundant between flies raised on poor versus standard diet (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of targeted metabolomics data.

claim: 57 metabolites were differentially abundant between flies raised on poor versus standard diet at 10% FDR.
source: Of the 113 metabolites, 57 were found to be differentially abundant between Selected and Control flies at 10% FDR, and also 57 differentially abundant between flies raised on poor versus standard diet (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of targeted metabolomics data.

claim: Eight essential amino acids were less abundant in Selected than Control flies.
source: Evolutionary adaptation to larval malnutrition resulted in a striking shift in proteinogenic amino acid concentrations in adult flies: eight essential amino acids were less abundant in the Selected than Control flies, while the reverse was the case for four non-essential ones (Figure 2Bi).
evidence: Based on targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 2Bi.

claim: Four non-essential amino acids were more abundant in Selected than Control flies.
source: Evolutionary adaptation to larval malnutrition resulted in a striking shift in proteinogenic amino acid concentrations in adult flies: eight essential amino acids were less abundant in the Selected than Control flies, while the reverse was the case for four non-essential ones (Figure 2Bi).
evidence: Based on targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 2Bi.

claim: Multiple purine compounds were less abundant in Selected than Control flies.
source: Multiple purine compounds were less abundant in the Selected than Control flies, including both purine nucleobases and nucleosides, and the electron carriers NAD, NADP, and FAD; an exception is ADP, which was more abundant in the Selected flies (Figure 2Bii; ATP was not reliably quantified).
evidence: Based on targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 2Bii.

claim: ADP was more abundant in Selected flies compared to Control flies.
source: Multiple purine compounds were less abundant in the Selected than Control flies, including both purine nucleobases and nucleosides, and the electron carriers NAD, NADP, and FAD; an exception is ADP, which was more abundant in the Selected flies (Figure 2Bii; ATP was not reliably quantified).
evidence: Based on targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 2Bii.

claim: Selected flies had lower levels of trehalose than Controls.
source: Selected flies had lower levels of trehalose (the principal sugar circulating in hemolymph) and of lactate than Controls (Figure 2Biv), but higher concentrations of compounds linking glycerol with glycolysis, with no indication of differences in concentration of upstream and downstream glycolysis intermediates (Figure 2Biv).
evidence: Based on targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 2Biv.

claim: Selected flies had lower levels of lactate than Controls.
source: Selected flies had lower levels of trehalose (the principal sugar circulating in hemolymph) and of lactate than Controls (Figure 2Biv), but higher concentrations of compounds linking glycerol with glycolysis, with no indication of differences in concentration of upstream and downstream glycolysis intermediates (Figure 2Biv).
evidence: Based on targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 2Biv.

claim: Selected flies show accumulation of medium chain (C6–C12) acyl-carnitines compared to Controls.
source: Compared to the Controls, the Selected flies show accumulation of medium chain (C6–C12) acyl-carnitines (Figure 2Bv).
evidence: Based on targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 2Bv.

claim: Acyl-carnitines with long-chain (C16–C18) residues were less abundant in Selected than Control flies.
source: In contrast, acyl-carnitines with long-chain (C16–C18) residues, which are typical for insect triglycerides (Stanley-Samuelson et al., 1988), were less abundant in the Selected than Control flies (Figure 2Bv).
evidence: Based on targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 2Bv, with reference to Stanley-Samuelson et al., 1988.

claim: The evolutionary and phenotypically plastic responses to the poor larval diet were largely additive with no significant interaction.
source: We detected no interaction between the evolutionary regime and current diet either in the PCA-MANOVA (Wilks' λ = 0.59, F6,5 = 0.6, p = 0.41) or in the gene-by-gene analysis (lowest q = 99.9%). Thus, both the evolutionary adaptation and the phenotypically plastic response to larval diet experienced had substantial effects on adult gene expression patterns; however, these effects appeared largely additive (i.e., independent of each other).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of gene expression data using PCA-MANOVA and gene-by-gene analysis.

claim: The plastic response of adult gene expression to larval undernutrition did not in general predict the evolutionary response.
source: Thus, except for genes involved in the cuticle maturation, the plastic (within-generation) response of adult gene expression pattern to larval undernutrition did not in general predict the evolutionary, genetically based response. If anything, evolution tended on average to oppose phenotypically plastic responses of gene expression to larval diet.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of gene expression changes shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The correlation between the main effect of diet and the main effect of evolutionary regimes across all genes was weakly negative (r = −0.22, p < 0.0001, N = 8701).
source: Across all genes, the correlation between the main effect of diet and the main effect of evolutionary regimes was weakly negative (r = −0.22, p < 0.0001, N = 8701; Figure 4A), as was the corresponding correlation for genes annotated to metabolism (GO metabolic process, r = −0.26, p < 0.0001, N = 4606).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The evolutionary change of metabolome driven by larval diet paralleled the phenotypically plastic response to some degree.
source: By contrast, the evolutionary change of metabolome driven by larval diet did to some degree parallel the phenotypically plastic response (correlation across all metabolites r = 0.32, p = 0.0005, N = 113; Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of metabolite abundance data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Of 30 metabolites significant at 10% FDR for both evolutionary regime and diet treatment, 25 showed the same sign of difference.
source: Of the 30 metabolites that were significant at 10% FDR for both evolutionary regime and diet treatment, 25 showed the same sign of the difference between Selected and Control flies as the difference between flies raised on the poor versus standard diet (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.0005).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of metabolite abundance data using Fisher's exact test.

claim: The difference in metabolite abundance between Selected and Control populations in adults was positively correlated with the analogous difference in larvae (r = 0.37, p = 0.0002).
source: Across all metabolites, the difference in metabolite abundance between the Selected and Control populations in the adults was positively correlated with the analogous difference in the larvae (r = 0.37, p = 0.0002; Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis comparing adult and larval metabolomics data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Of 424 genes differentially expressed at nominal p < 0.05 between Selected and Controls at both adults and larvae, 377 (89%) showed the same direction of change.
source: Of 424 genes that were differentially expressed at nominal p < 0.05 between Selected and Controls at both adults and larvae (Supplementary file 5), 377 (89%) showed the same direction of change on poor diet, more than expected at random (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.0001, Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on comparison of adult and larval gene expression data using Fisher's exact test, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The estimates of log-fold change in gene expression were correlated across all 8437 genes shared between adult and larval data sets (r = 0.35, p < 0.0001).
source: The estimates of log-fold change were even correlated across all 8437 genes shared between the data sets (r = 0.35, p < 0.0001; Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of adult and larval gene expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Of 39 metabolites affected by both starvation treatment and evolutionary regime, 29 showed the same direction of change.
source: Of 39 metabolites affected by both starvation treatment and the evolutionary regime, 29 showed the same direction of change between fed and starved flies as between Control and Selected flies, significantly more than expected by chance (p = 0.006, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of metabolomics data using Fisher's exact test.

claim: 74 metabolites were differentially abundant between fed and starved flies at 10% FDR.
source: Of the 113 metabolites, 74 were detected to be differentially abundant (at 10% FDR) between fed and starved flies (in terms of the main effect of starvation treatment in the full factorial model, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of metabolomics data with FDR correction.

claim: For six essential amino acids, the response to starvation differed between Selected and Control flies.
source: However, the focus on the main effects of starvation treatment on amino acid abundance is somewhat misleading because for 6 of the 10 essential amino acids the response to starvation differed between the Selected and Control flies.
evidence: Based on analysis of metabolomics data showing significant regime × starvation interaction.

claim: Fed flies from Selected populations were situated closer to starved flies along the starvation-loaded PC1 axis than fed Control flies.
source: Rather, fed flies from the Selected populations were situated closer to starved flies along the starvation-loaded PC1 axis than fed Control flies (Figure 6A; F1,17.8 = 14.0, p = 0.0015, GMM on PC1 scores); in the starved condition, they converged to a similar state (F1,17.8 = 0.0, p = 0.99; see Supplementary file 7 for detailed statistics).
evidence: Based on PCA analysis of metabolomics data shown in Figure 6A and statistical testing using GMM.

claim: Selected females laid only about 2/3 of the number of eggs produced by Control females when both were raised on poor larval diet.
source: Despite having evolved under these conditions, Selected females laid only about 2/3 of the number of eggs produced by the Control females, whose ancestors did not face the poor larval diet (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on fecundity measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Poor diet-raised females of Selected populations tended to have slightly fewer ovarioles than their Control counterparts.
source: Indeed, we found that poor diet-raised females of the Selected populations tended to have slightly fewer ovarioles than their Control counterparts (Figure 7B).
evidence: Based on ovariole count measurements shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Even adjusted for the difference in ovariole number, Selected flies produced substantially fewer eggs than Controls.
source: However, even adjusted for the difference in ovariole number, the Selected flies produced substantially fewer eggs than Controls (Figure 7C).
evidence: Based on analysis of eggs per ovariole shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Larvae of Selected populations evolved higher viability, faster development and faster growth on the poor diet compared to Controls.
source: Compared to the Controls, larvae of the Selected populations evolved higher viability, faster development and faster growth on the poor diet (Kolss et al., 2009; Vijendravarma and Kawecki, 2013; Cavigliasso et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Selected larvae appear to invest more in protein digestion.
source: The Selected larvae appear to invest more in protein digestion (Erkosar et al., 2017), are more efficient in extracting amino acids from the poor diet (Cavigliasso et al., 2020), and are able to initiate metamorphosis at a smaller size (Vijendravarma et al., 2012), traits that likely contribute to their improved performance on the poor diet.
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Selected larvae are more efficient in extracting amino acids from the poor diet.
source: The Selected larvae appear to invest more in protein digestion (Erkosar et al., 2017), are more efficient in extracting amino acids from the poor diet (Cavigliasso et al., 2020), and are able to initiate metamorphosis at a smaller size (Vijendravarma et al., 2012), traits that likely contribute to their improved performance on the poor diet.
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Selected larvae are able to initiate metamorphosis at a smaller size.
source: The Selected larvae appear to invest more in protein digestion (Erkosar et al., 2017), are more efficient in extracting amino acids from the poor diet (Cavigliasso et al., 2020), and are able to initiate metamorphosis at a smaller size (Vijendravarma et al., 2012), traits that likely contribute to their improved performance on the poor diet.
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Selected populations evolved reduced dependence on microbiota for development on poor diet.
source: The Selected populations also evolved reduced dependence on microbiota for development on poor diet (Erkosar et al., 2017), However, they show greater susceptibility to an intestinal pathogen (Vijendravarma et al., 2015) and are less resistant than Controls to starvation at the adult stage (Kawecki et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Selected populations show greater susceptibility to an intestinal pathogen.
source: The Selected populations also evolved reduced dependence on microbiota for development on poor diet (Erkosar et al., 2017), However, they show greater susceptibility to an intestinal pathogen (Vijendravarma et al., 2015) and are less resistant than Controls to starvation at the adult stage (Kawecki et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Selected populations are less resistant than Controls to starvation at the adult stage.
source: The Selected populations also evolved reduced dependence on microbiota for development on poor diet (Erkosar et al., 2017), However, they show greater susceptibility to an intestinal pathogen (Vijendravarma et al., 2015) and are less resistant than Controls to starvation at the adult stage (Kawecki et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Selected and Control larvae show divergence in metabolite abundance consistent with evolutionary changes in amino acid metabolism.
source: Finally, the Selected and Control larvae also show divergence in metabolite abundance consistent with evolutionary changes in amino acid metabolism, with lower free amino acid concentrations and a higher rate of amino acid catabolism (Cavigliasso et al., 2023).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Evolutionary divergence between Selected and Control populations is highly polygenic, involving over 100 genomic regions.
source: Evolutionary divergence between Selected and Control populations is highly polygenic, involving over 100 genomic regions enriched in hormonal and metabolic genes (Kawecki et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Prenatal undernutrition in humans is correlated with negative consequences for diverse aspects of metabolic function and health at old age.
source: In humans, prenatal undernutrition is correlated with negative consequences for diverse aspects of metabolic function and health at old age (Roseboom et al., 2006; de Rooij et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Prolonged nutrient shortage at a juvenile stage usually results in stunted adult size.
source: Prolonged nutrient shortage at a juvenile stage usually results in stunted adult size, but also often has profound effects on adult physiology that do not seem mediated by body size.
evidence: Based on general scientific knowledge about developmental nutrition effects.

claim: Juvenile undernutrition has lasting effects on adult metabolism of affected individuals.
source: Juvenile undernutrition has lasting effects on adult metabolism of the affected individuals, but it is unclear how adult physiology is shaped over evolutionary time by natural selection driven by juvenile undernutrition.
evidence: Based on general scientific knowledge about developmental nutrition effects.

claim: Experimental evolution studies that compared plastic and evolutionary responses of gene expression to novel environments usually found little overlap between genes involved in the two responses.
source: In particular, experimental studies that compared plastic and evolutionary responses of gene expression to novel environments usually found little overlap between genes involved in the two responses; for those that did overlap, evolutionary change tended to counter rather than be in line with plasticity (Yampolsky et al., 2012; Ghalambor et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2016) for an exception, see Josephs et al., 2021.
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Most metabolic genes in Drosophila are expressed at both larval and adult stages.
source: For example, while some enzymes in Drosophila have distinct larval and adult forms encoded by different genes, most metabolic genes are expressed at both stages (https://flybase.org/).
evidence: Based on information from FlyBase database.

claim: Fecundity in Drosophila is limited by essential amino acids.
source: Fecundity in Drosophila is limited by essential amino acids (Grandison et al., 2009), in particular those in short supply relative to the needs of fly protein synthesis, which for a yeast-based diet are methionine and leucine (Piper et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Several essential amino acids act as signaling molecules that promote protein synthesis by activating TOR complex 1.
source: In addition, several essential amino acids (methionine, valine, isoleucine, and in particular leucine, all less abundant in Selected flies) act as signaling molecules that promote protein synthesis by activating TOR complex 1 (Wolfson et al., 2016; Antikainen et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2022).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Most of the protein synthesis activity in adult female fat bodies is directed toward synthesizing egg proteins.
source: Most of the protein synthesis activity in adult female fat bodies is directed toward synthesizing egg proteins (Piper et al., 2017; Gupta et al., 2022).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Uric acid is the main compound in which nitrogen is excreted in insects.
source: As adults, larvae of Selected populations also show lower abundances than Control larvae of multiple amino acids, including six essential, and a higher concentration of uric acid (Cavigliasso et al., 2023), an end product of purine metabolism and the main compound in which nitrogen is excreted in insects (Salway, 2018; Cohen et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Increased catabolism of amino acids sourced from autophagy is one of the hallmarks of the physiological response to starvation.
source: Increased catabolism of amino acids – sourced from autophagy – is one of the hallmarks of the physiological response to starvation (Scott et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Drosophila are 'income breeders' in that they directly convert acquired nutrients into eggs rather than relying on previously accumulated reserves.
source: Drosophila are 'income breeders' in that they directly convert acquired nutrients into eggs rather than relying on previously accumulated reserves (O'Brien et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: The number of ovarioles is determined during larval development.
source: The rate of egg production may thus be limited by the number of ovarioles (Schmidt et al., 2005), which is determined during larval development (Bergland et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: The fat body is the key metabolic organ in Drosophila, combining the functions of mammalian liver and adipose tissue.
source: We focused on female abdominal fat body, the key metabolic organ combining the functions of mammalian liver and adipose tissue.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Drosophila anatomy and physiology.

claim: Metabolic reserves of glycogen and triglycerides are stored and mobilized in the fat body.
source: It is in the fat body where metabolic reserves of glycogen and triglycerides are stored and mobilized, and where dietary nutrients are converted into the proteins and lipids subsequently transported to the ovaries for egg production (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: Dietary nutrients are converted into proteins and lipids in the fat body and subsequently transported to the ovaries for egg production.
source: It is in the fat body where metabolic reserves of glycogen and triglycerides are stored and mobilized, and where dietary nutrients are converted into the proteins and lipids subsequently transported to the ovaries for egg production (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on previously published studies cited in the text.

claim: The metabolic profile of Selected flies resembled that of flies subject to starvation even when well fed.
source: Even when well fed, the metabolic profile of Selected flies resembled that of flies subject to starvation.
evidence: Based on comparison of metabolomics data between Selected flies and starved flies.

claim: Selected flies had lower reproductive output than Controls even when both were raised under the conditions under which the Selected populations evolved.
source: Finally, Selected flies had lower reproductive output than Controls even when both were raised under the conditions under which the Selected populations evolved.
evidence: Based on fecundity measurements shown in Figure 7.

claim: Evolutionary adaptation to juvenile undernutrition has large pleiotropic consequences for adult metabolism that are costly rather than adaptive for adult fitness.
source: These results imply that evolutionary adaptation to juvenile undernutrition has large pleiotropic consequences for adult metabolism, and that they are costly rather than adaptive for adult fitness.
evidence: Based on integration of gene expression, metabolomics, and fecundity data.

claim: Juvenile and adult metabolism do not appear to evolve independently from each other even in a holometabolous species where the two life stages are separated by a complete metamorphosis.
source: Thus, juvenile and adult metabolism do not appear to evolve independently from each other even in a holometabolous species where the two life stages are separated by a complete metamorphosis.
evidence: Based on the correlation of evolutionary changes between larval and adult stages.

claim: The evolved differences in adult gene expression and metabolite abundance between Selected and Control populations were positively correlated with the corresponding differences previously reported for Selected versus Control larvae.
source: The evolved differences in adult gene expression and metabolite abundance between Selected and Control populations were positively correlated with the corresponding differences previously reported for Selected versus Control larvae. This implies that genetic variants affect both stages similarly.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis comparing adult and larval data.

claim: Genetic variants favored by selection on larvae likely had pleiotropic effects on gene expression at both larval and adult stages.
source: Such a similarity would be expected either if both life stages were exposed to similar selection pressures or if genetic variants favored by larval undernutrition had pleiotropic effects on gene expression at the two stages. As we argue in 'Discussion,' we find the latter interpretation more parsimonious, even it contradicts the notion that larval and adult gene expression patterns can be decoupled from each other in holometabolous insect (Moran, 1994; Rolff et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on logical inference from the correlation between larval and adult evolutionary changes.

claim: Most changes in adult physiology of Selected populations primarily reflect pleiotropic effects of genetic variants that improve larval growth and survival on the poor diet.
source: In contrast, if the metabolic changes observed at the adult stage primarily reflect pleiotropic effects of genetic variants that improve larval growth and survival on the poor diet, Selected adults should not have an advantage or even be inferior to Controls even when raised under the conditions under which the former evolved.
evidence: Based on the finding that Selected adults have lower fecundity than Controls even on poor diet.

claim: The similarity in evolutionary changes between larvae and adults is more likely due to pleiotropic effects of genetic variants than to similar selection pressures at both stages.
source: However, it seems difficult to conceive why such compensatory responses of a well-fed adult should be mediated by similar physiological adjustments as those that promote larval growth under severe undernutrition. A more plausible explanation for the similarity in evolutionary changes between larvae and adults is that most genetic variants available for evolution affected gene expression of larvae and adults similarly.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about the mechanisms underlying correlated evolutionary changes.

claim: Many of the adult gene expression changes represent correlated responses to selection on the larval stage rather than direct response to selection on adult performance.
source: As a consequence, many of the adult gene expression changes would represent correlated responses to selection on the larval stage rather than the direct response to selection on adult performance (Lande and Arnold, 1983).
evidence: Based on inference from the similarity of larval and adult evolutionary changes and evolutionary theory.

claim: The lower abundance of most essential amino acids in Selected flies is consistent with their lower fecundity.
source: Thus, while we have not demonstrated a direct causal link, lower abundance of most essential amino acids in the Selected flies is consistent with their lower fecundity.
evidence: Based on inference connecting metabolite abundance data with fecundity measurements.

claim: The differences in amino acid abundance between Selected and Control populations appear consistent with differential use of amino acids in metabolism rather than differences in dietary acquisition or protein synthesis.
source: Thus, rather than being explained by differences in dietary amino acid acquisition or use in protein synthesis, the differences in amino acid abundance between Selected and Control populations appear consistent with differential use of amino acids in metabolism.
evidence: Based on inference from the pattern of amino acid abundance changes.

claim: Selected larvae likely catabolize amino acids and excrete nitrogenous waste products at a higher rate than Control larvae.
source: This suggests that Selected larvae catabolize amino acids and excrete nitrogenous waste products at a higher rate, a hypothesis further supported by their increased accumulation of the heavy isotope of nitrogen 15N (Cavigliasso et al., 2023).
evidence: Based on inference from metabolite abundance patterns and isotope data.

claim: It is possible that Selected flies catabolize amino acids and excrete uric acid at a higher rate than Controls also at the adult stage.
source: Thus, while we do not have direct evidence for this, it remains possible that Selected flies catabolize amino acids and excrete uric acid at a higher rate than Controls also at the adult stage.
evidence: Based on speculation from indirect evidence about amino acid metabolism.

claim: Selected populations may have become programmed to express a starved-like adult metabolic phenotype as a by-product of genetic adaptation to poor larval diet.
source: It is tempting to speculate that, as a by-product of genetic adaptation to poor larval diet, the Selected populations have become programmed to express a starved-like adult metabolic phenotype, which might explain their low fecundity.
evidence: Based on speculation connecting metabolic profile similarity to starvation with fecundity reduction.

claim: Assessing the adaptive nature of phenotypically plastic responses based on the direction of evolutionary change may be misleading.
source: These considerations imply that assessing the adaptive (or otherwise) nature of phenotypically plastic responses based on the direction of the evolutionary change may be misleading.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about the interpretation of plasticity-evolution relationships.

claim: Independent evolution of larval and adult metabolism would require independent regulation of expression of the same genes.
source: Thus, independent evolution of larval and adult metabolism would require independent regulation of expression of the same genes. It may be more parsimonious to expect that most regulatory genetic variants would tend to affect gene expression across lifetime, constraining independent evolution of the juvenile and adult stages.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about gene regulation and evolutionary constraints.

claim: If most regulatory genetic variants affect gene expression across lifetime, response to selection driven by juvenile undernutrition would lead to similar physiological change in larvae and adults.
source: It may be more parsimonious to expect that most regulatory genetic variants would tend to affect gene expression across lifetime, constraining independent evolution of the juvenile and adult stages. If so, response to selection driven by juvenile undernutrition would lead to similar physiological change in larvae and adults, and these changes might be disadvantageous for adult performance, in particular under conditions of plentiful food.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the consequences of pleiotropic gene regulation.

claim: The fecundity reduction in Selected adults represents a significant fitness trade-off of the improved ability of Selected larvae to survive and develop under extreme nutrient shortage.
source: Thus, the fecundity reduction we found in Selected adults represents a significant fitness trade-off of the improved ability of the Selected larvae to survive and develop under extreme nutrient shortage.
evidence: Based on inference connecting larval adaptation benefits with adult fecundity costs.

claim: The genomic architecture of differentiation between Selected and Control populations includes many candidate genes for starvation resistance.
source: Consistent with the link with starvation, the genomic architecture of differentiation between the Selected and Control populations includes many candidate genes for starvation resistance (Kawecki et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on previously published genomic analysis cited in the text.

claim: All populations were derived from the same base population originally collected in 1999 in Basel, Switzerland.
source: Six Selected and six Control populations were all derived from the same base population originally collected in 1999 in Basel (Switzerland) and maintained on the standard food for several years before the evolution experiment started in 2005 (Kolss et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The evolution experiment started in 2005.
source: Six Selected and six Control populations were all derived from the same base population originally collected in 1999 in Basel (Switzerland) and maintained on the standard food for several years before the evolution experiment started in 2005 (Kolss et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: RNAseq was performed on 4-day-old adult females from Selected and Control populations raised on either larval diet.
source: To explore plastic and evolutionary responses of adult gene expression to poor diet, we performed RNAseq on 4-day-old adult females from the Selected and Control populations raised on either larval diet.
evidence: Stated directly in the Results section describing the experimental design.

claim: Flies were mated and reproductively active prior to collection for RNAseq.
source: Prior to collection for RNAseq, the flies were transferred to standard diet upon emergence from the pupa and maintained in mixed-sex group; thus, they were mated and reproductively active.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The standard diet consisted of 12.5 g dry brewer's yeast, 30 g sucrose, 60 g glucose, 50 g cornmeal, and other ingredients per liter of water.
source: The 'standard' diet consisted of 12.5 g dry brewer's yeast, 30 g sucrose, 60 g glucose, 50 g cornmeal, 0.5 g CaCl2, 0.5 g MgSO4, 10 ml 10% Nipagin, 6 ml propionic acid, 20 ml ethanol, and 15 g of agar per liter of water.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The poor diet contained 1/4 of the concentrations of yeast, sugars, and cornmeal compared to the standard diet.
source: The 'poor' diet contained 1/4 of the concentrations of yeast, sugars, and cornmeal, but the same concentrations of the other ingredients.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Metabolite abundance was measured using multiple pathway targeted analysis in the carcasses of 4-day-old mated females.
source: Metabolite abundance was measured using multiple pathway targeted analysis in the carcasses of 4-days-old mated females obtained as described above.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 113 metabolites were retained after filtering for data quality.
source: After filtering for data quality, we retained 113 metabolites that were quantified (normalized to protein content) in all samples.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Samples were analyzed by hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (HILIC-MS/MS).
